source_text: Καὶ γὰρ, ὅπερ ἔμπροσθεν ἔλεγον, τοῦτο καὶ νῦν λέγω, καὶ λέγων οὐ παύσομαι, ὅτι οὐχ ἡ διδασκαλία μόνον, οὐδὲ ἡ παραίνεσις καὶ συμβουλὴ, ἀλλὰ καὶ αὕτη ἡ ὄψις τῶν ἁγίων πολλὴν εἶχεν ἡδονὴν καὶ ὠφέλειαν, καὶ αὐτὸς δὲ τῶν ἱματίων ὁ στολισμὸς, καὶ αὐτὸς τῶν ὑποδημάτων ὁ τρόπος. Καὶ γὰρ ἐντεῦθεν πολλή τις εἰς τὸν ἡμέτερον εἰσενήνεκται βίον ὠφέλεια, τὸ μαθεῖν μέχρι ποῦ τοῖς ἀναγκαίοις ἐχρῶντο. Οὐδὲ γὰρ μόνον τὸ μέτρον οὐχ ὑπερέβαινον τῆς χρείας, ἀλλ' ἔστιν ὅπου οὔτε τῆς χρείας αὐτῆς ἀπέλαυον ἁπάσης· ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐν λιμῷ καὶ δίψει καὶ γυμνότητι διετέλεσαν. Καὶ τοῖς μὲν μαθηταῖς ἐπιτάττων ὁ Παῦλος ἔλεγεν· Ἔχοντες τροφὰς καὶ σκεπάσματα, τούτοις ἀρκεσθησόμεθα· περὶ δὲ ἑαυτοῦ φαίνεται λέγων, ὅτι Ἄχρι τῆς ἄρτι ὥρας καὶ πεινῶμεν, καὶ διψῶμεν, καὶ γυμνητεύομεν, καὶ κολαφιζόμεθα. Ἀλλὰ γὰρ ἃ μεταξὺ ἔλεγον, καὶ μετὰ ταῦτα εἰσῆλθεν, ἀναγκαῖον εἰς μέσον παραθεῖναι πολλὴν ἔχοντα τὴν ζήτησιν. Τί δὲ τοῦτό ἐστιν; Ἔλεγον, ὅτι καὶ ὁ τῶν ἀποστολικῶν ἱματίων στολισμὸς παρέχει πολλὴν ἡμῖν τὴν ὠφέλειαν· μεταξὺ δέ με ταῦτα λέγοντα εἰσῆλθεν ὁ νόμος τοῦ Χριστοῦ, ὃν ἔθηκεν αὐτοῖς, οὕτω λέγων· Μὴ κτήσησθε χρυσὸν, μηδὲ ἄργυρον, μηδὲ χαλκὸν εἰς τὰς ζώνας ὑμῶν, μηδὲ ὑποδήματα, μηδὲ ῥάβδον εἰς τὴν ὁδόν· φαίνεται δὲ Πέτρος σανδάλια ἔχων. Ὅτε γοῦν ὁ ἄγγελος καθεύδοντα αὐτὸν ἐξύπνισε, καὶ ἐξήγαγε τοῦ δεσμωτηρίου, φησίν· Ὑπόδησαι τὰ σανδάλιά σου, καὶ περιβαλοῦ τὸ ἱμάτιόν σου, καὶ ἀκολούθει μοι. Καὶ Παῦλος δὲ Τιμοθέῳ γράφων λέγει· Τὸν φελόνην, ὃν ἀπέλιπον ἐν Τρωάδι παρὰ Κάρπῳ, φέρε ἐρχόμενος, καὶ τὰ βιβλία, μάλιστα τὰς μεμβράνας. Τί λέγεις; ὁ Χριστὸς οὐδὲ ὑποδήματα ἐκέλευσεν ἔχειν, καὶ σὺ φελόνην ἔχεις, καὶ ἕτερος σανδάλια πάλιν; Καὶ εἰ μὲν τῶν εὐτελῶν τινες ἦσαν, καὶ τῶν οὐ πάντοτε τῷ Διδασκάλῳ πειθομένων, οὐκ ἦν ζήτημα τὸ λεγόμενον· ἐπειδὴ δὲ οἱ καὶ τὰς ψυχὰς ἑαυτῶν ἐπιδιδόντες, καὶ κορυφαῖοι καὶ πρῶτοι τῶν μαθητῶν εἰσιν οὗτοι, καὶ πάντα ἐπείθοντο τῷ Χριστῷ, ὁ δὲ Παῦλος οὐ μόνον τὰ ἐπιταττόμενα ἐποίει, ἀλλὰ καὶ ὑπὲρ τὰ σκάμματα ἐπεπήδα, κἀκείνου κελεύοντος ἐκ τοῦ Εὐαγγελίου ζῇν, οὗτος ἐκ τῶν χειρῶν αὐτοῦ ἔζη, πλέον τι τῶν ἐπιτεταγμένων ποιήσας, ἄξιον ὄντως ζητῆσαι, τίνος ἕνεκεν, πάντα αὐτῷ πειθόμενοι, ἐνταῦθα δοκοῦσι παραβαίνειν αὐτοῦ τὸν νόμον. Ἀλλ' οὐ παραβαίνουσιν. Οὐδὲ γὰρ εἰς τοῦτο χρήσιμος ἡμῖν οὗτος ἔσται μόνον ὁ λόγος, εἰς τὴν ὑπὲρ τῶν ἁγίων ἐκείνων ζήτησιν, ἀλλὰ καὶ εἰς τὸ τὰ τῶν Ἑλλήνων ἐμφράξαι στόματα. Καὶ γὰρ πολλοὶ χηρῶν οἰκίας ἀνατρέποντες, ὀρφανοὺς γυμνοῦντες, τὰ πάντων περιβαλλόμενοι, λύκων οὐδὲν ἄμεινον διακείμενοι, ἐκ τῶν ἀλλοτρίων ζῶντες πόνων, ὁρῶντες πολλάκις τινὰς τῶν πιστῶν δι' ἀῤῥωστίαν σώματος πλείονα περιβεβλημένους ἱμάτια, τὸν νόμον εὐθέως ἡμῖν τοῦ Χριστοῦ προβάλλονται, καὶ ταῦτα λέγουσι τὰ ῥήματα· Οὐκ ἐκέλευσεν ὑμῖν ὁ Χριστὸς μὴ ἔχειν δύο χιτῶνας, μηδὲ ὑποδήματα; πῶς οὖν ὑμεῖς παραβαίνετε τὸν νόμον τὸν περὶ τούτων κείμενον; Εἶτα δαψιλὲς γελάσαντες καὶ ἀνακαγχάσαντες, καὶ καταισχύναντες τὸν ἀδελφὸν, ἀποπηδῶσιν. Ἵν' οὖν μὴ ταῦτα γένηται, φέρε καὶ τὴν ἐκείνων ἀναισχυντίαν ἐπιστομίσωμεν.
thought_title: The apostles' clothing seems to break Christ's command
orientation: Chrysostom is defending the apostles against the charge that they disobeyed Christ's command to possess nothing, after having praised the very sight and clothing of the saints as beneficial.
pass_a_gloss: For indeed, what I was saying before, this also now I say, and saying I will not stop, that not only the teaching, nor the exhortation and counsel, but also this very sight of the saints had much pleasure and benefit, and the very adornment of the garments, and the very manner of the sandals. For indeed from this much benefit has been brought into our life, the learning to what extent they used necessary things. For not only did they not exceed the measure of need, but there are cases where they did not even enjoy all of the need itself; but also in hunger and thirst and nakedness they continued. And commanding the disciples Paul said: Having food and coverings, with these we shall be content; but about himself he appears saying, that Until the present hour we both hunger, and thirst, and are naked, and are struck. But indeed what I was saying in between, and after these things it entered, it is necessary to set before you in the midst, having much inquiry. And what is this? I was saying, that also the adornment of the apostolic garments provides much benefit to us; but in between, as I was saying these things, the law of Christ entered, which he laid down for them, saying thus: Do not acquire gold, nor silver, nor bronze for your belts, nor sandals, nor a staff for the road; but Peter appears having sandals. When indeed the angel woke him sleeping, and led him out of the prison, he says: Put on your sandals, and wrap your cloak around you, and follow me. And Paul writing to Timothy says: The cloak, which I left in Troas with Carpus, bring when you come, and the books, especially the parchments. What do you say? Christ commanded not even to have sandals, and you have a cloak, and another has sandals again? And if they were some of the common sort, and of those not always obeying the Teacher, the thing said would not be a question; but since those who even give up their own souls, and are the leaders and first of the disciples, these men, and they obeyed Christ in everything, and Paul not only did the things commanded, but also leaped beyond the lines, and while that one commanded to live from the Gospel, this one lived from his own hands, doing more than the things commanded, it is truly worthy to inquire, for what reason, obeying him in everything, they seem here to transgress his law. But they do not transgress. For not only for this will this argument be useful to us, for the inquiry on behalf of those holy men, but also for stopping the mouths of the Greeks. For indeed many who overturn the houses of widows, stripping orphans, putting on themselves the things of all, disposed no better than wolves, living from the labors of others, seeing often some of the faithful because of weakness of body wrapped in more garments, immediately throw at us the law of Christ, and say these words: Did not Christ command you not to have two tunics, nor sandals? How then do you transgress the law laid down about these things? Then having laughed abundantly and guffawed, and having shamed the brother, they leap away. So that these things may not happen, come let us stop up their shamelessness.

choices.why: Chrysostom is praising the very clothing of the saints as beneficial; 'adornment' captures the positive, deliberate quality of their dress without implying luxury

choices.english: did not exceed the measure of need
choices.why: The phrase 'measure of need' preserves the idea of a limit or standard (μέτρον) that they did not cross
This is a proverbial athletic image of going beyond the marked bounds; keeping 'lines' preserves the metaphor of the jumping pit
The verb means literally to put something in the mouth; 'stop up' keeps the forceful, physical image of silencing
The compound verb intensifies the laughter; 'guffawed' conveys loud, mocking laughter

pass_b_english: For what I was saying before, I say again now, and I will not stop saying it: not only their teaching, not only their exhortation and counsel, but even the very sight of the holy ones carried great pleasure and benefit—even the adornment of their clothes, even the manner of their sandals. From this, you see, a great benefit has been brought into our own life: learning how far they went in using necessities. They not only did not exceed the measure of need, but sometimes they did not even have the full measure of need itself; they persevered in hunger and thirst and nakedness. And when Paul commanded the disciples, he said, "Having food and covering, with these we will be content" (1 Timothy 6:8). But about himself he appears to say, "To this present hour we hunger and thirst and are naked and are beaten" (1 Corinthians 4:11).

But what I was saying in between—and what came to my mind afterward—I must set before you, since it involves a great deal of inquiry. What is this? I was saying that even the adornment of the apostles' clothes provides us great benefit. But while I was saying these things, the law of Christ came to my mind, the law he laid down for them, saying, "Do not acquire gold, or silver, or copper for your belts, or sandals, or a staff for the road" (Matthew 10:9-10). Yet Peter appears to have sandals. At any rate, when the angel woke him from sleep and led him out of the prison, he says, "Put on your sandals, and wrap your cloak around you, and follow me" (Acts 12:8). And Paul, writing to Timothy, says, "Bring the cloak that I left in Troas with Carpus when you come, and the books, especially the parchments" (2 Timothy 4:13).

What are you saying? Christ commanded them not even to have sandals, and you have a cloak, and another has sandals again? Now if they were some of the ordinary people, some of those who did not always obey the Teacher, what was said would not be a question. But since these are the very ones who gave up their own lives, the leaders and first of the disciples, and they obeyed Christ in everything—and Paul not only did what was commanded but even leaped beyond the lines, for while Christ commanded living from the gospel, this man lived by his own hands, doing more than what had been ordered—it is truly worth asking why, though they obeyed him in everything, they seem here to transgress his law.

But they do not transgress it. And this discussion will be useful to us not only for the inquiry on behalf of those holy ones, but also for stopping up the mouths of the Greeks. For many who overturn widows' houses, strip orphans bare, wrap themselves in everyone's property, and behave no better than wolves, living from the labors of others—when they often see some of the faithful wearing more clothes because of bodily weakness, they immediately throw Christ's law at us and say these words: "Did not Christ command you not to have two tunics, or sandals? How then do you transgress the law laid down about these things?" Then, after laughing lavishly and guffawing, and shaming the brother, they leap away. So that this may not happen, come, let us stop up their shamelessness.

problems.why: "Struck" is too weak; κολαφίζομαι means buffeted, struck with fists, or beaten—physical abuse, not mere striking.

problems.quote: he lived from his own hands
problems.source_quote: οὗτος ἐκ τῶν χειρῶν αὐτοῦ ἔζη
problems.why: Missing crucial contrast: "while Christ commanded... this man lived from his own hands"—the Greek emphasizes Paul's voluntary extra effort.
problems.fix: this man lived by his own hands

problems.quote: If we have food and covering, with these we will be content
problems.source_quote: Ἔχοντες τροφὰς καὶ σκεπάσματα, τούτοις ἀρκεσθησόμεθα
problems.why: Source is a command/imperative: 'Having food and covering, we will be content with these.' English 'If we have' makes it conditional.
problems.fix: Having food and covering, with these we will be content
problems.ruling: Ἔχοντες is participial, not conditional; 'If we have' changes grammar and softens command.

fixed: κολαφιζόμεθα means buffeted/beaten with fists, so 'beaten' is more accurate than 'struck'.
The Greek οὗτος ἐκ τῶν χειρῶν αὐτοῦ ἔζη emphasizes Paul's voluntary extra effort; 'this man lived by his own hands' captures the contrast better.
The source is a participial command, not a conditional: 'Having food and covering, with these we will be content.'

problems.quote: for while Christ commanded him to live from the gospel
problems.source_quote: κἀκείνου κελεύοντος ἐκ τοῦ Εὐαγγελίου ζῇν
problems.why: 'him' is wrong — the Greek has 'κελεύοντος' (commanding, genitive absolute), with no explicit object. Christ commanded this generally (to apostles), not specifically Paul. The English makes it seem like a personal command to Paul.
problems.fix: for while Christ commanded living from the gospel

problems.quote: they did not even enjoy the full measure of need itself
problems.source_quote: οὔτε τῆς χρείας αὐτῆς ἀπέλαυον ἁπάσης
problems.why: 'enjoy' is wrong for ἀπέλαυον. They did not 'have the benefit of' or 'partake of' the full measure — it's about possession/use, not pleasure. And 'full measure' reverses the sense: 'ἁπάσης' goes with 'τῆς χρείας' (all of need itself), meaning they lacked even the complete basic necessity.
problems.fix: they did not even have the full measure of need itself
problems.ruling: ἀπέλαυον means 'enjoyed/partook of'; 'full measure' for ἁπάσης with χρείας means 'all of need,' not 'full measure.'

problems.why: 'clearly says' overstates φαίνεται λέγων ('appears to be saying'). The Greek is softer, indicating apparent meaning from context, not clarity.
problems.ruling: φαίνεται λέγων means 'appears to be saying,' not 'clearly says'; changes evidential to emphatic.

problems.why: Same issue: 'clearly has' for 'φαίνεται... ἔχων' ('appears to have'). The Greek is evidential, not emphatic.
problems.fix: Yet Peter appears to have sandals
problems.ruling: φαίνεται δὲ Πέτρος means 'Peter appears,' not 'clearly has'; softens evidential force, key to argument.

problems.why: In this idiom ψυχή means 'life,' not 'soul'; 'gave up their own souls' misleads readers into thinking they forfeited their eternal souls.
problems.ruling: ἐπιδιδόντες τὰς ψυχάς ἑαυτῶν is lay-down-one's-life idiom; 'souls' suggests forfeiture, not risked lives.

problems.quote: while I was saying these things, the law of Christ came in
problems.source_quote: μεταξὺ δέ με ταῦτα λέγοντα εἰσῆλθεν ὁ νόμος τοῦ Χριστοῦ
problems.why: εἰσῆλθεν with accusative με means 'occurred to me / entered my mind'; 'came in' misses the idiom and drops the personal reference.
problems.fix: while I was saying these things, the law of Christ came to my mind
problems.ruling: μεταξὺ με … εἰσῆλθεν: με plus εἰσῆλθεν means occurred to me; English drops με and reads as law intruding.

problems.quote: But what I was saying in between—and it came in after these things—it is necessary to set before you
problems.source_quote: Ἀλλὰ γὰρ ἃ μεταξὺ ἔλεγον, καὶ μετὰ ταῦτα εἰσῆλθεν, ἀναγκαῖον εἰς μέσον παραθεῖναι
problems.why: εἰσῆλθεν here also means 'came to mind'; 'it came in after these things' is confusing and obscures that Chrysostom is introducing a thought that occurred to him.
problems.fix: But what I was saying in between—and what came to my mind afterward—I must set before you
problems.ruling: μετὰ ταῦτα εἰσῆλθεν is thought occurred; 'came in after' confuses timing and hides mental interruption.

last_rejected.quote: "Having food and covering, with these we will be content" (1 Timothy 6:8)
last_rejected.source_quote: Ἔχοντες τροφὰς καὶ σκεπάσματα, τούτοις ἀρκεσθησόμεθα
last_rejected.why: This quote is from 1 Timothy 6:8, but Paul commands the disciples here; Chrysostom attributes it to Paul commanding disciples, suggesting the Gospel commission context.
last_rejected.fix: Cite 1 Timothy 6:8 or note the parallel with Luke 3:14 / 1 Tim 6:8.
last_rejected.ruling: Chrysostom explicitly says 'τοῖς μαθηταῖς ἐπιτάττων ὁ Παῦλος ἔλεγεν'—Paul commanding disciples. 1 Timothy 6:8 is Paul's own instruction, fitting the context of apostolic teaching to disciples. The citation is correct.

last_rejected.quote: living from the labors of others
last_rejected.why: Greek says 'living from others' labors'—'labors' is πόνων, correct. No error.
last_rejected.ruling: ἐκ τῶν ἀλλοτρίων πόνων ζῶντες = 'living from others' labors'; English matches source exactly.

last_rejected.quote: Did not Christ command you not to have two tunics, or sandals?
last_rejected.source_quote: Οὐκ ἐκέλευσεν ὑμῖν ὁ Χριστὸς μὴ ἔχειν δύο χιτῶνας, μηδὲ ὑποδήματα;
last_rejected.why: The objector's quote adds 'two tunics' (δύο χιτῶνας) which is NOT in Chrysostom's earlier quote of Christ's law. Chrysostom earlier quoted Christ saying 'no sandals, no staff.' The objector introduces 'two tunics'—this is the objector's words, not Chrysostom's quote. The English correctly attributes this to 'they say these words.' However, checking if 'two tunics' appears in Matthew 10:10—yes, in Luke 9:3 and parallel passages. The objector is conflating or citing from memory. The English is accurate to the source. No error.
last_rejected.ruling: δύο χιτῶνας μηδὲ ὑποδήματα correctly rendered; objector's words faithfully translated from source.
